summary: The blocks between Market Street and the waterfront came back from the fire with machinery inside them. Building after building appears in the record holding a permit for an engine, a boiler and an oil tank, and the permits say what the machines were for: a hat factory at 583 Market Street, a candy factory at 49 Fremont Street, brass being melted at 83 Natoma Street and at 225 Beale Street. Rail came in behind them. One firm after another was allowed to run a siding off the Southern Pacific's tracks and into its own doors — the Enterprise Brewing Company off Harrison Street in 1908, A. Schilling & Co. on Second Street in 1916, Zellerbach Paper off Front Street in 1923, the Palmolive Company on Second Street the same year — and in 1907 the Santa Fe was granted a right of way on Spear Street, from Little Main Wharf to Mission Street. The roadways were repaved with basalt blocks on concrete, and in 1908 the Board ordered the owners of the Pacific Building to stop putting a canopy out over the sidewalk until it had worked out whether they were allowed to — the first of many arguments here about the sidewalk. That same autumn it went after the tents: "under the guise and name of clairvoyants, test mediums and fortune tellers, numerous persons have erected unsightly tents on various portions of Montgomery avenue, Kearny street and Market street." Sidewalk widths were then fixed street by street in law, twenty feet along the Embarcadero, fifteen on Post Street, and at the end of the twenties the Board began dividing the kerb doorway by doorway, writing a directory of downtown as it went: 225 Bush Street, thirty-six feet, the Standard Oil Building; 155 Sansome Street, thirty-six feet, the stock exchange, two elevators; 27 Geary Street, eighteen feet, the Owl Drug Company, one elevator. In 1943 Grant Avenue between Bush Street and Broadway was renamed Mei-Ling Way for Madame Chiang Kai-shek. In 1947 the city counted more than sixteen hundred people crossing one half-hour stretch of Montgomery Street sidewalk; in 1949 it abandoned its plans to widen California Street and Post Street, and went at the car in bulk instead — a study in 1950 found a twelve-hundred-car garage would pay for itself in a single downtown block, and by 1953 the Board was weighing a plan for one of three thousand seven hundred and fifty stalls on Mission Street between Third and Fourth. After that the ground went the other way: Powell Street closed to cars in 1972, tables and chairs licensed in Maiden Lane at lunchtime from 1973 — a permit still being amended in 2025 — while the towers went up behind hoardings the Board granted one street at a time, Sacramento Street for the Levi Strauss building, Front Street for the Embarcadero Center's walkways. In 1982 it started writing the old buildings down instead: the Phelan and the Flatiron on Market Street, the Kohl Building on Montgomery the year after. On the South Beach side the same ground was replanned and sold as flats — the Rincon Point and South Beach plan widened in 1992, sixty-two units at 401 Main Street in 1994 — and lately the Board has kept at the Transbay blocks, taken progress reports on retrofitting 301 Mission Street, and gone back to naming: the Allegory of California mural at 155 Sansome Street in 2021, One Montgomery Street, the old Crocker bank, in 2022. In between it decides, week by week, who may sell a drink and where: a wine bar in the Mira on Folsom Street, a lounge at 88 Kearny Street, a shop at 221 Sansome Street.
